results.title: U.S. Treasury Markets: The High-Frequency Evidence
results.content: # U.S. Treasury Markets: The High-Frequency Evidence. **U.S. Treasury Markets: The High-Frequency Evidence**. This paper reviews the existing empirical evidence on the time-series behavior of the U.S. Treasury markets at high frequency: daily and intra-day data. The use of high-frequency data in econometric analyses is a major recent development in the study of the fixed income markets: the response of prices to scheduled and unscheduled news, conditional-volatility dynamics, and jump and diffusion behavior, can all be examined much more precisely with high-frequency data. High-frequency data are also important for the characterization of the trading environment as they allow us to examine the immediate impact of trading on prices and how this impact is affected by the presence of macro news. ### U.S. Treasury Markets: The High-Frequency Evidence - Introduction. This chapter reviews the existing empirical evidence on the time-series behavior of the U.S. Treasury markets at high frequency: daily and intra-day data. We believe that the use of high-frequency data in econometric analyses is a major recent development in the study of the fixed income markets, and has important implications for our understanding of how financial markets work. The response of prices to scheduled and unscheduled news, for example, can be examined much more precisely with high-frequency data, by isolating behavior within narrow windows surrounding the news releases. One can also take advantage of high-frequency data in the study of conditional-volatility dynamics, by relating volatility to macro news and intra-day seasonal patterns, and by constructing realized-volatility measures that approximate the true volatility process as sampling becomes more frequent. By using high-frequency data it is also possible to examine the immediate impact of trading on prices and how this impact is affected by the presence of macro news. Indeed, several studies using high-frequency data for the U.S. Treasury markets have appeared during the last two decades and this is an ideal moment to review them. We then focus on literature covering the following four topics: i) the reaction of prices and rates to macroeconomic news; ii) market micro-structure effects; iii) bond risk premia; and iv) the effects of high frequency trading.3;4 Each section concludes with a brief summary of the main results reviewed. results.content: > *Time Series Analytics with Snowflake and FactSet Tick Data: A Practical Quickstart*. > *In this hands-on guide, I explore how Snowflake’s advanced SQL features streamline financial time series analytics using FactSet Tick Data. This project is the first part of a larger series where I build a robust time-series analysis workflow from data ingestion to building a front-end Streamlit app. In this article, I cover key Snowflake capabilities such as TIME\_SLICE, ASOF JOIN , and windowing functions like RANGE BETWEEN, all applied to real-world trade and quote data. Whether you're a data engineer, financial analyst, or someone exploring the Snowflake Marketplace, this guide will help you understand how to derive meaningful insights while optimizing performance and storage in time-series analysis.*. > *The architecture of this solution is designed to unlock deep financial insights from high-frequency trading data using the modern capabilities of Snowflake’s data cloud.*. This dataset provides millisecond-level trade and quote data across multiple securities, enabling precise analysis.*. > Aggregates trades into fixed-width time buckets (e.g., weekly) for performance summaries of average\_price and total\_volume.*. > Joins each trade to its most recent quote or closing price using Snowflake’s ASOF JOIN, essential for transaction cost analysis and slippage measurement.*. > Applies windowed aggregation functions like AVG() and SUM() with RANGE BETWEEN to compute rolling statistics (e.g., moving averages), which are more resilient to gaps in time-series data.*. > *Aggregating Time-Series Data using TIME\_SLICE*. For instance, when working with FactSet Tick History data — where every trade or quote may be recorded to the second — it becomes essential to downsample the data to make it more interpretable and performant for analysis.*. This allows all records within that time window to be grouped together, enabling me to apply aggregate functions such as* `AVG()` *for price or* `SUM()` *for volume.*. > *In my analysis of financial tick data, I often needed to* ***combine trades with the most recent available quote****. > *To solve this, I used* ***Snowflake’s ASOF JOIN construct****, which is purpose-built for* ***aligning time-series data that do not match perfectly on timestamps****. > *To make time-series financial data truly accessible to non-technical users, I integrated Snowflake Cortex Analyst into a custom-built Streamlit web application.

results.title: Resampling High-Frequency Timestamps with Pandas for Real-Time Systems | by Bhagya Rana | Medium
results.content: # **Resampling High-Frequency Timestamps with Pandas for Real-Time Systems**. ## **How I Solved Data Granularity Chaos and Enabled Stable Insights in a Real-Time Monitoring Pipeline**. *Learn how to use Pandas to resample high-frequency timestamp data for real-time systems — achieve smoother trends, better performance, and clearer insights.*. When I first started working on a real-time system for IoT sensor data, I hit a wall. The sheer volume wasn’t the problem — Pandas could handle the size. But when it came to summarizing this data across time intervals to power dashboards and alerts, our results became jittery, inconsistent, and downright confusing. That’s when I discovered the real power of **resampling high-frequency timestamps in Pandas** — a quiet but potent feature that can make or break your time-series data pipeline. In this article, I’ll break down the strategy I used to tame noisy high-frequency data, create consistent intervals, and ensure our real-time monitoring system stayed fast, accurate, and actionable.
